title: Competent general machine intelligence

concept.text: Competent general machine intelligence is a system that performs at least as well as the median skilled adult across most cognitive tasks and can learn unfamiliar tasks. The target combines breadth with a defined level of performance: excellence in a few activities would not establish general competence. Morris, Legg and coauthors include learning new skills within generality and do not require a robot body or physical execution.

This entry additionally proposes that the capability reside in one agent, or one coherently trained family, that can learn an unfamiliar cognitive job from ordinary instructions, documentation, practice and feedback, then sustain specified multi-day projects without a person repairing its intermediate steps. These are proposed requirements for this innovation. Morris and coauthors distinguish cognitive capability from autonomy, so sustained independent execution adds a separate requirement to their definition of Competent AGI.

significance.text: If achieved, broad competence combined with transferable learning and sustained independent execution could make many computer-based professional tasks delegable to a general system, including unfamiliar work for which no separate application had been engineered. The revolutionary change would be demonstrated adaptability across kinds of work, rather than isolated success on a particular benchmark. Human-comparable performance would apply within the demonstrated scope and conditions; it would not establish universal professional reliability.

Economic disruption and faster scientific work are conditional downstream possibilities. They would depend on effective deployment, adoption, suitable interfaces and validation for particular jobs. Morris and coauthors explicitly distinguish technical capability from realized economic value and warn that interface limitations can reduce deployed performance. Passing a broad evaluation would therefore provide evidence for delegation, but would not by itself establish dependable performance in every workplace.

Scope synthesis: this capability would not automatically confer physical autonomy, machine-checked mathematical truth or a guarantee that the system pursues a specified goal. Those are distinct advances represented elsewhere in the supplied roster. Nor would skilled-adult cognitive competence alone guarantee scientific breakthroughs: discovery also depends on evidence, experiments, resources and successful use of the system.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central capability to establish is the combination of broad skilled-adult performance, learning of unfamiliar work and reliable transfer beyond narrowly selected tasks. Morris and coauthors identify unresolved questions about how to measure generality, including what proportion of a benchmark would suffice. They also explain why some framings of the Turing test are inadequate: convincing conversational behavior does not establish the required breadth or level of cognitive performance.

Engineering synthesis: this entry's additional autonomy requirement demands dependable execution across many linked decisions. A convincing system would need to retain relevant context, coordinate tools and intermediate work, detect consequential errors, recover from setbacks and incorporate feedback without hidden human repair. The supplied evidence does not identify a single missing algorithm or establish that any particular architecture can supply this combination. The challenge is to demonstrate the integrated behavior under realistic conditions.

A separate measurement barrier is distinguishing general capability from familiarity with test material and favorable task selection. Evaluations need representative cognitive and metacognitive work, meaningful skilled-human comparisons, interactive tasks and tests of new skill acquisition. Morris and coauthors envisage open-ended and interactive evaluation, while leaving the sufficient coverage of an AGI benchmark unresolved. This supports the need for broader evidence without establishing that no accepted sufficient benchmark exists as of November 2026.

current_state.text: Morris and coauthors classified Competent AGI as not yet achieved in their assessment of systems as of September 2023. Their paper was first posted on 4 November 2023, revised on 5 January 2024 and published at ICML 2024. That historical classification grounds the capability target but is not a measurement of systems available on 1 November 2026.

Kwa and coauthors' software-task study, first posted on 18 March 2025 and identified in the supplied research as a NeurIPS 2025 paper revised on 10 July 2026, provides narrower quantitative evidence. The landing-page abstract retained in the supplied review reports a roughly 50-minute 50%-task-completion horizon for Claude 3.7 Sonnet. This expresses task difficulty in terms of the time humans take to complete tasks at which the model succeeds about half the time; it does not measure how long the agent itself can operate autonomously, and it does not establish broad occupational competence.

The revised paper abstract retained in the review instead highlights o3 with a roughly 110-minute 50% horizon. That result concerns a different model and does not contradict the Claude 3.7 Sonnet figure. The supplied review had only partial paper evidence: the PDF extraction ends during page 40, and numerical plots were not inspected. The exact Claude horizon therefore rests on the retained landing-page abstract rather than independent graphical verification.

METR's retained tracker was last updated on 8 September 2026 and states that it is no longer actively updated. It warns that measurements above 16 hours are unreliable with its current task suite and that its reporting is not a complete record of the most capable models. The 16-hour warning is a limitation of measurement with that suite, not a demonstrated upper bound on model capability. Although the retained page text was complete, the review did not inspect values in its interactive graphs.

The supplied research describes OpenAI's GDPval as an evaluation of one-shot economic knowledge work that omits context-building and ambiguous real jobs. However, no GDPval artifact was retained for the supplied review, so those descriptions and limitations remain unverified here. This access gap limits the weight GDPval can carry in this record; it is not evidence that the descriptions are false.

Evidence synthesis: none of the source material assessed in the supplied review demonstrates the proposed combination of broad skilled-adult competence, unfamiliar occupation acquisition and sustained multi-day execution without human repair. That observation is confined to this evidence set. The empty freshness-search record, incomplete METR model coverage and unavailable GDPval artifact prevent a conclusion that no public system met the target as of 1 November 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: an independent evaluator would publish and preregister the evaluation protocol before the evaluated training run, while protecting the actual test instances from training exposure. The battery would cover previously unseen software work, mathematics, scientific reasoning and a representative range of other cognitive and metacognitive activities. It would include interactive and open-ended work alongside tasks with objectively checkable outcomes. Systems would receive tools and interfaces comparable to those available to the human comparison group.
completion_criteria.label: Training-protected preregistered battery of unseen cognitive work with comparable tools

completion_criteria.text: Proposed passing criteria would combine median-or-better skilled-adult performance on a majority of the battery, acquisition of one unfamiliar occupation from documentation and feedback without a new foundation-model training run, and completion of specified multi-day projects without human repair. Task sampling, weighting, reliability requirements, permitted assistance and occupation-acquisition success would be defined in advance. Passing most tasks by excelling in one heavily represented domain would not adequately test the intended breadth.
completion_criteria.label: Majority at median-or-better skilled-adult level, learned occupation, unrepaired multi-day projects

completion_criteria.text: The skilled-human comparison and emphasis on broad task coverage follow the Morris framework, but the proposed majority threshold is not an established sufficient test of AGI. Morris and coauthors leave the necessary proportion unresolved and anticipate a very high percentage. Their inclusion of interactive tasks and learning supports evaluating more than one-shot leaderboard performance; it does not validate this entry's particular protocol or passing line.
completion_criteria.label: Note, not a test: the majority pass line is this entry's own

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: independent evaluators would repeat the assessment with fresh protected instances, additional tester-selected tasks and unfamiliar projects. Reports would disclose the evaluated system or family, tool access, human interventions, resource budgets, failure rates and variability across runs. Results would establish demonstrated breadth under those conditions, not literal universality. Job-specific validation would still be needed before extending the conclusion to different interfaces, levels of assistance or deployment environments.
completion_criteria.label: Independent fresh repeats disclose evaluation conditions and demonstrated breadth

related_concepts.text: Roster-based scope comparison: CSC-08, General-purpose physical autonomy in unmodified environments, overlaps in adaptable behavior and sustained execution but adds perception and physical action in real environments. CSC-03 concerns cognitive work and does not require embodiment. CSC-07, Reliable machine-checked mathematical discovery, overlaps with mathematical reasoning but requires discoveries whose validity can be checked formally. General cognitive competence alone would not establish that specialized capability. These distinctions follow the supplied titles and scope descriptions; full records for the other entries were not supplied.

Roster-based scope comparison: CSC-10, Machine-checked behavioral guarantees for frontier learned models, concerns guarantees about behavior rather than demonstrated cognitive competence. CSC-04, Industrial-cost proof-carrying software, similarly concerns software accompanied by checkable assurances. A competent general system might help produce proofs or software, but successful task performance would not itself provide either kind of guarantee.

Roster-based scope comparison: CSC-06, A predictive theory of generalization for modern learning systems, could inform the design and evaluation of systems that learn unfamiliar work. It is a theoretical target distinct from demonstrating a competent general agent: a theory need not deliver such an agent, and a successful agent would not by itself establish a predictive theory.

Roster-based scope comparison: CSC-01, Practical polynomial-time algorithms for NP-complete problems, and CSC-02, Application-scale fault-tolerant quantum computation, concern algorithms and computing capabilities. CSC-03 does not imply efficient solutions to NP-complete problems or fault-tolerant quantum hardware, and those advances alone would not demonstrate general cognitive competence.

Roster-based scope comparison: CSC-05, Routine-cost general computation on encrypted data, and CSC-09, Practical indistinguishability obfuscation, concern privacy and cryptographic protection of computation or programs. They could complement the deployment of general intelligence, but cognitive competence does not establish their efficiency or security properties. Each remains a separate innovation.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not settle whether any public system met this entry's combined target as of 1 November 2026.
The representative task distribution, weighting and sufficient proportion of successes for broad competence remain unresolved; a majority threshold is only a proposal.
The meaning of one coherently trained family needs operational definition, including limits on task-specific routing, adaptation and separately trained specialists.
Occupation acquisition and multi-day autonomy need predefined success, assistance, reliability and resource criteria.
GDPval's scope and limitations remain unverified because no artifact was supplied.
The exact Claude 3.7 Sonnet horizon was not independently verified from numerical plots; the retained abstract supports the reported approximate value.
Full records for the related roster entries were not supplied, so comparisons are limited to their titles and the scope distinctions present in the research and review.

brief.title: A machine that can learn and do most mental work
possible: You could hand over unfamiliar computer-based work with instructions, documentation and feedback. The same system, or a coherently trained family of systems, could learn the job and carry projects through several days without someone repairing the steps along the way.
why: People could delegate many professional tasks without needing a separate application built for each job. The change would come from a system that adapts across kinds of work and performs at least as well as a typical skilled adult on most mental tasks.

sources.who: Meredith Ringel Morris and colleagues at Google DeepMind
sources.showed: They proposed a framework that separates breadth of ability, level of performance and independence. It includes learning new skills within general competence.
sources.cited_for: Their framework defines the broad skilled-adult capability target.
sources.not_established: A framework does not demonstrate a system that combines broad competence, learning unfamiliar work and independent execution.

sources.who: Meredith Ringel Morris and colleagues at Google DeepMind
sources.showed: An earlier version of the same work.

sources.who: Thomas Kwa and colleagues at Model Evaluation & Threat Research
sources.showed: In a preprint, they found that AI systems could complete increasingly difficult software tasks, measured against skilled humans' completion times. Performance was lower on messier tasks.
sources.quote:
We also find evidence that AI agent time
horizons can differ by a large factor depending on the task domain and reference human population.
sources.cited_for: Their study measures progress on extended software work using human comparisons.
sources.not_established: Software-task success does not establish broad professional competence or dependable execution over several days.

sources.showed: Their measurements compare AI success with the time human experts need for software-related tasks. They also found that performance drops substantially when judged as a whole rather than by automatic scoring.
sources.quote: In our original time horizon paper, we found that AI agents did worse on messier tasks.
sources.cited_for: Their results distinguish success on clearly specified tasks from performance in messier work.
sources.not_established: These measurements do not establish capability across mental work or measure how long a system can operate independently.

sources.showed: GDPval is an evaluation of economic knowledge work completed in a single attempt.
sources.cited_for: It addresses performance on economically relevant tasks.
sources.not_established: Single-attempt work does not establish learning an unfamiliar occupation or completing projects over several days.

shown: METR has measured progress on extended software tasks against skilled human performance. Its study found that systems could handle increasingly difficult tasks, while struggling more with messy work.

These results demonstrate narrower abilities. They do not establish the combination of broad skilled-adult performance, learning an unfamiliar job and completing projects over several days without human repair.
missing: A system would need to combine broad skilled-adult performance with the ability to learn unfamiliar work.
It would need to manage context, tools, errors and setbacks across projects lasting several days without human repair.
Tests would need to distinguish transferable ability from familiar test material and favorable task selection.

milestones.label: A broad unseen test with comparable tools
milestones.explanation: Independent evaluators would publish the protocol before training and protect unseen tasks spanning reasoning, learning and interactive work, with comparable tools for humans. This would test breadth beyond familiar material.

milestones.label: Broad skilled performance, a learned job and independent projects
milestones.explanation: A system would meet predefined criteria: typical skilled-adult performance on most tasks, learning an unfamiliar occupation without foundation retraining, and multi-day projects without human repair. This would test the combined capability.

milestones.label: The proposed majority pass line remains unsettled
milestones.explanation: Passing most tasks would remain a proposed threshold rather than an established sufficient test of general competence. The required breadth of success is still unresolved.

milestones.label: Independent repeats establish breadth under disclosed conditions
milestones.explanation: Independent evaluators would repeat tests with fresh protected tasks and unfamiliar projects, disclosing tools, assistance, resources and failures. This would establish reproducibility and the conditions under which competence holds.

uncertain: Which tasks, weights and proportion of successes would establish broad competence?
What limits on specialist systems and task-specific adaptation would make a family count as a coherent system?
What assistance, resources and reliability would count as learning an occupation and sustaining independent work?

page.title: Competent artificial general intelligence
page.definition: One AI system performs at least as well as the median adult with the relevant skill on most tasks across a wide range of non-physical activities. These include learning new skills and judging when to ask for help. Such judgments require metacognition, the ability to assess one's own reasoning and its limits.

goal.need: Workers in 44 predominantly digital US occupations earn about $3 trillion a year. The value of AI assistance varies even within one profession. In a consulting trial, AI users completed tasks 25.1% faster on average across 18 tasks, yet were 19 percentage points less likely to solve a separate managerial problem correctly. An assistant that could learn unfamiliar parts of an assignment could save professionals time across more of their work, provided checking and correcting its output took less time than doing the work themselves.

completion.title: An AI meets the median-skilled-adult criterion across cognitive and metacognitive tasks.
completion.criterion: Across a wide range of non-physical cognitive and metacognitive tasks, the same system reaches at least the 50th percentile of adults with the relevant skill on most tasks. Assessment includes learning new skills and recognizing when to ask for help. The proposed benchmark would include new tasks supplied by testers. The task distribution and exact proportion sufficient for Level 2 remain open.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas fallback. Google DeepMind defines the Level 2 performance threshold. No outside body has specified a complete pass rule calibrated to that level.
completion.threshold_quote: at least 50th percentile of skilled adults
completion.basis: DeepMind defines the comparator for each task and describes broad coverage on a changing set of tasks. ARC-AGI-2 and GDPval test parts of that range. A Definition of AGI uses a different cognitive score. None supplies the missing breadth rule for Level 2.

milestones.title: An AI algorithm reaches 75% human-normalized performance on a majority of 49 Atari games.
milestones.criterion: Use the same learning algorithm, architecture and hyperparameters across all 49 Atari games. Separate training for each game is allowed. Average the agent's score over 30 episodes per game, each lasting up to five minutes, with randomized starts. On at least 25 games, score at least 75 on the scale 100 × (agent score − random score)/(professional games tester's score − random score), using the published human and random baselines.
milestones.set_by: Google DeepMind researchers, the evaluation protocol and Figure 3 caption in Human-level control through deep reinforcement learning; this threshold concerns Atari games.
milestones.threshold_quote: (that is, operationalized as a level of 75% or above) in the majority of games.

milestones.title: An AI reaches the ARC Prize 2025 target of 85% on private ARC-AGI-2 tasks under competition limits.
milestones.criterion: Score at least 85% on the 120-task private ARC-AGI-2 evaluation under the 2025 Kaggle compute limits, with no internet access. Each test input allows two predictions and requires an exact output grid. Release the reproducible code and methods under the competition's licensing terms before receiving the final private score. The organizer describes the efficiency target as approximately US$2.50 per task.
milestones.set_by: ARC Prize, the 2025 competition's published objective and Grand Prize conditions; this threshold concerns novel grid-transformation tasks.
milestones.threshold_quote: Reach 85% accuracy on the ARC-AGI-2 private evaluation dataset within the Kaggle efficiency limits

milestones.title: An AI reaches GDPval's 50% reference line for wins or ties against professional work.
milestones.criterion: Use GDPval's 220-task gold subset, with five tasks from each of 44 occupations. Generate three deliverables per prompt and have three occupational experts independently grade each against the human deliverable in blinded comparisons. Count a win or tie when the expert rates the model's work better than or as good as the human's. Wins plus ties must reach 50% of comparisons across the subset.
milestones.set_by: OpenAI, GDPval gold-subset protocol and the 50% reference line in Figure 5. The percentage counts comparisons of deliverables.

milestones.title: An agent scores 100% on the ARC Prize 2026 interactive ARC-AGI-3 evaluation.
milestones.criterion: Score 100% on the official ARC-AGI-3 evaluation with an eligible 2026 Kaggle submission. The agent interacts with unfamiliar environments without instructions. It must complete every level and reach the full score in every environment under the published scoring rule, which weights level scores and compares actions used with human action counts. Run offline within the competition's compute limits and release the code and methods as open source.
milestones.set_by: ARC Prize, 2026 ARC-AGI-3 Grand Prize conditions and ARC-AGI-3 scoring protocol.
milestones.threshold_quote: Awarded to the first eligible agent that scores 100% on the ARC-AGI-3 evaluation.

milestones.title: One system matches an unskilled human across a wide range of non-physical tasks.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate Emerging AGI, Level 1 in the Levels of AGI framework. Across a wide range of non-physical tasks, including learning new skills, the same system performs at least as well as an unskilled human on most tasks. The framework gives examples of qualifying systems and leaves the benchmark and exact breadth cutoff unspecified.
milestones.set_by: Google DeepMind, qualitative Level 1 classification in Levels of AGI, Table 1, also used in Organizing Intelligence.
milestones.threshold_quote: Equal to or somewhat better than an unskilled human

not_found: A complete benchmark and sufficiency rule calibrated to DeepMind's Competent AGI level were not located.

goal.need = "Workers in 44 predominantly digital US occupations earn about $3 trillion a year. The value of AI assistance varies even within one profession. In a consulting trial, AI users completed tasks 25.1% faster on average across 18 tasks, yet were 19 percentage points less likely to solve a separate managerial problem correctly. An assistant that could learn unfamiliar parts of an assignment could save professionals time across more of their work, provided checking and correcting its output took less time than doing the work themselves.". Reason: The current paragraph describes a benchmark without explaining where AI assistance saves professionals time or why its uneven performance matters.

edit completion: criterion = "Across a wide range of non-physical cognitive and metacognitive tasks, the same system reaches at least the 50th percentile of adults with the relevant skill on most tasks. Assessment includes learning new skills and recognizing when to ask for help. The proposed benchmark would include new tasks supplied by testers. The task distribution and exact proportion sufficient for Level 2 remain open."; set_by = "Technology Atlas fallback. Google DeepMind defines the Level 2 performance threshold. No outside body has specified a complete pass rule calibrated to that level."; threshold_quote = "at least 50th percentile of skilled adults"; threshold_ref = 4; basis = "DeepMind defines the comparator for each task and describes broad coverage on a changing set of tasks. ARC-AGI-2 and GDPval test parts of that range. A Definition of AGI uses a different cognitive score. None supplies the missing breadth rule for Level 2.". Reason: DeepMind specifies a performance floor on most tasks and calls for newly added tasks, while leaving the exact breadth cutoff unresolved.

edit m1: criterion = "Use the same learning algorithm, architecture and hyperparameters across all 49 Atari games. Separate training for each game is allowed. Average the agent's score over 30 episodes per game, each lasting up to five minutes, with randomized starts. On at least 25 games, score at least 75 on the scale 100 \u00d7 (agent score \u2212 random score)/(professional games tester's score \u2212 random score), using the published human and random baselines.". Reason: The Atari criterion mixes a published result into the test and omits the duration and randomized starts of the evaluation episodes.

edit m2: criterion = "Score at least 85% on the 120-task private ARC-AGI-2 evaluation under the 2025 Kaggle compute limits, with no internet access. Each test input allows two predictions and requires an exact output grid. Release the reproducible code and methods under the competition's licensing terms before receiving the final private score. The organizer describes the efficiency target as approximately US$2.50 per task.". Reason: The 2025 ARC criterion includes the winning score and its publication status alongside the conditions for a qualifying submission.

edit m3: criterion = "Use GDPval's 220-task gold subset, with five tasks from each of 44 occupations. Generate three deliverables per prompt and have three occupational experts independently grade each against the human deliverable in blinded comparisons. Count a win or tie when the expert rates the model's work better than or as good as the human's. Wins plus ties must reach 50% of comparisons across the subset."; set_by = "OpenAI, GDPval gold-subset protocol and the 50% reference line in Figure 5. The percentage counts comparisons of deliverables."; threshold_quote = "Parity with Industry Expert"; threshold_ref = 1. Reason: The GDPval criterion needs the figure's reference-line label and the sampling procedure that determines what counts as one comparison.
